issues.legal_issue: An arbitration award that makes a party’s relinquishment of an interest in immovable property conditional on payment, without itself creating or extinguishing that interest, does not require compulsory registration.
material_facts: The award stated that one heir would give up her interest in the property only after receiving a specified payment.
Until payment, that heir could continue occupying the portion of the house in her possession.
The High Court declined to make the award a rule of the court because it was unregistered.
issues.conclusion: The award did not create or extinguish a right in immovable property and therefore did not require compulsory registration; the award could be made a rule of the court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of a non-testamentary instrument that itself creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes a qualifying right in immovable property. An award that only quantifies the value of an existing entitlement and makes relinquishment conditional on payment does not itself create or extinguish that right. The Court relied on Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar, Upendra Nath Bose v. Lall, and Sheonarain Lal v. Rameshwari Devi, and distinguished Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit.

predicates.arbitration_award_proceeding: The dispute was referred to arbitration and the court considered whether the resulting award could be made a rule of the court.
predicates.relinquishment_conditional_on_payment: The award made a party’s relinquishment of an interest in property conditional on that party first receiving payment.
predicates.award_does_not_itself_change_property_ri: The award described an existing property entitlement and the method for working it out, rather than itself creating or extinguishing a property right.

issues.definition: When an arbitration award makes relinquishment conditional on payment and does not itself change property rights, it does not require compulsory registration.

issues.legal_issue: An award cannot be remitted to the arbitrator to address a registration matter that is unrelated to the arbitrator’s decision on the merits, and the court cannot use the provisions for correcting an imperfect award when the award is not imperfect.
material_facts: The objection concerned registration of the award, not the legality of the arbitrator’s decision on the merits.
The registration issue did not arise from or affect the decision contained in the award.
The award was not found to be imperfect, and there was no request to extend the time for registration.
issues.conclusion: The award could not be remitted under section 16(1)(c), and there was no basis to exercise powers under section 15(b) of the Arbitration Act or section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 15(b) and 16(1)(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, the court may act on an imperfect award or remit an award for reconsideration where the matter is connected with the arbitrator’s decision. A matter unrelated to that decision, such as the fact of registration, is not a ground for remittal. The Court relied on Rikhabdass v. Ballabhdas and Nani Bala Saha v. Ram Gopal Saha.

predicates.arbitration_award_court_proceeding: A court was asked to act on an arbitration award in proceedings concerning whether it could be made a rule of the court.
predicates.objection_is_unrelated_to_merits: The objection concerned a matter that did not form part of or affect the arbitrator’s decision on the merits.
predicates.award_is_not_imperfect: The award was not shown to be imperfect in a way that required correction.

issues.definition: In court proceedings concerning an arbitration award, an unrelated objection cannot support remittal or correction when the award is not imperfect.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s mental incapacity to participate in arbitration is not established where the evidence shows that the party understood the proceedings, participated consciously, and could manage ordinary responsibilities.
material_facts: A party was alleged to have been mentally incapable of participating in the arbitration.
The evidence indicated that she could perform personal duties satisfactorily and intelligently, had participated in the proceedings, and understood what was happening in court.
She accepted the award of her own free will, and the Court found no sufficient basis to disagree with the lower court’s assessment.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim that the party was mentally incapable of participating in the arbitration.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the party’s actual understanding, participation, and functional abilities on the evidence before it; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: arbitration_capacity_dispute and party_understood_proceedings and party_participated_consciously and party_showed_functional_capacity

predicates.arbitration_capacity_dispute: A party’s capacity to participate in arbitration was challenged in proceedings concerning the award.
predicates.party_understood_proceedings: The party showed an understanding of what was happening during the proceedings.
predicates.party_participated_consciously: The party took part in the arbitration proceedings consciously.
predicates.party_showed_functional_capacity: The evidence showed that the party could manage ordinary responsibilities satisfactorily and intelligently.

issues.definition: When a party to arbitration understood the proceedings, participated consciously, and showed functional capacity, the asserted incapacity is not established.

issues.legal_issue: In an appeal under Article 136, the Court may adjust monetary terms of an award to protect the interests of the parties where changed living costs make the existing provision inadequate.
material_facts: The award set a monthly maintenance payment and specified lump sums for contingencies affecting the parties’ interests in the property.
The Court considered inflation and the rise in the cost of living and concluded that the specified amounts were inadequate.
The matter was before the Court in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The Court modified the award by increasing the maintenance and specified lump-sum payments, making the award as modified a rule of the court.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court must, so far as practicable, protect the interests of all parties. Applying that principle to inflation and the rise in the cost of living, the Court adjusted the award’s monetary terms.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The matter was before the Supreme Court in an appeal invoking its special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.award_sets_monetary_support_or_compensat: The award fixed monetary support or compensation for parties affected by its terms.
predicates.changed_living_costs_make_amounts_inadeq: The Court found that changed living costs had made the amounts in the award inadequate.

issues.definition: In an appeal under special appellate jurisdiction, where changed living costs make an award’s monetary provisions inadequate, the Court adjusts those provisions to protect the parties.
